title: Partition Strategies
description: Compare range-based, hash-based, and directory-based partitioning with real implementations in BigTable, DynamoDB, Cassandra, and HDFS.

segments.text: You've decided to partition your data. Good. Now comes the question that will haunt your on-call engineers for years: how do you decide which partition gets which data? Get this wrong, and you'll have one partition handling eighty percent of traffic while the others sleep. Let's look at three fundamental strategies.

Range-based partitioning assigns contiguous key ranges to partitions. Partition A gets keys A through F, Partition B gets G through M, and so on. BigTable and HBase use this approach. The massive advantage: range scans are efficient because nearby keys live on the same partition. Scanning all users with last names starting with S hits one partition.

The fatal flaw of range partitioning: hot spots from non-uniform key distributions. If your key is a timestamp, all writes go to the partition handling 'now.' That's every write in your system hitting one partition. HBase operators learn this lesson painfully when they use raw timestamps as row keys and one region server melts.

Hash-based partitioning fixes this. Hash the key, then assign hash ranges to partitions. MD5 of 'user_42' might map to partition three. DynamoDB and Cassandra use this approach. Keys distribute uniformly regardless of their natural ordering. No hot spots from skewed key distributions.
segments.thought_prompt: If hash-based partitioning distributes keys uniformly, what useful capability do you lose compared to range-based?

segments.text: You lose efficient range queries. In Cassandra, if you hash-partition by user_id, you can't do 'give me all users between ID 1000 and 2000' without hitting every partition. That query becomes a scatter-gather across all nodes. This is why Cassandra uses compound partition keys: hash the first part, range-sort within the partition.

Compound partition keys are the best of both worlds. In Cassandra, PRIMARY KEY of user_id and timestamp means user_id determines the partition through hashing, and timestamp sorts data within that partition. You can efficiently query 'all posts by user X in the last hour' because that's a range scan within a single partition.

Directory-based partitioning uses a lookup service that maps keys to partitions. HDFS NameNode does this: it knows exactly which DataNode holds each block. The directory gives you total flexibility to move data arbitrarily. But the directory itself becomes a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck.

Regardless of strategy, you need hot partition detection in production. Monitor partition-level metrics: request count, byte throughput, latency percentiles. DynamoDB CloudWatch gives you per-partition consumed capacity units. When one partition consistently exceeds others by three x or more, you have a hotspot that needs intervention.

Here's the decision matrix. Range-based: choose when you need range scans and can design keys to avoid hotspots. Hash-based: choose when uniform distribution matters more than range queries. Directory-based: choose when you need maximum flexibility and can afford the lookup service overhead. Most production systems use hash-based with compound keys.
segments.thought_prompt: Which strategy would you choose for a time-series IoT database with millions of devices?

segments.text: Your partition strategy is a foundational decision that's expensive to change later. It determines your query patterns, your hotspot risk, and your scaling characteristics. Choose based on your access patterns, not your data model. The data model should follow the partition strategy, not the other way around.
